tomato_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
tomato_healthy.homeRemedy: Keep up consistent watering right at the soil line (1-2 inches per week), avoid wetting the leaves, and mulch around the base with straw or shredded leaves to stop soil from splashing onto foliage. Give the plant 6-8 hours of direct sun and space plants 24-36 inches apart for airflow. Check the underside of a few leaves weekly for early pests or spots.
tomato_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. If growth looks slow, a balanced water-soluble fertilizer (e.g. 10-10-10 or a tomato-specific 18-18-21 blend) every 2-3 weeks during fruiting supports strong yields. A copper fungicide applied preventively every 7-10 days during long wet spells can help head off blight before it starts, especially if nearby plants have had disease before.

tomato_early_blight.cause: A fungus (Alternaria solani) that overwinters in soil and old plant debris, splashing onto the lowest, oldest leaves first during warm, humid weather - look for concentric 'target-ring' brown spots with yellowing around them.
tomato_early_blight.homeRemedy: Remove and bag (don't compost) any spotted leaves as soon as you see them, and mulch heavily around the base so rain can't splash spores from soil onto leaves. Space and stake plants for airflow, and water only at the soil line in the morning. A weekly spray of 1 tbsp baking soda + 2.5 tbsp vegetable or horticultural oil + 1 tsp liquid soap (not detergent) per gallon of water can slow mild infections - test on a couple of leaves first since baking soda can scorch foliage in hot sun.
tomato_early_blight.marketRemedy: Look for a fungicide labeled for early blight with chlorothalonil, mancozeb, or copper (copper hydroxide/copper octanoate) as the active ingredient - e.g. Bonide Fung-onil (chlorothalonil) or Southern Ag Liquid Copper Fungicide - applied every 7-10 days starting at the first sign of spots. Rotate between two different active ingredients (e.g. copper one week, chlorothalonil the next) to avoid resistance, and always check the pre-harvest interval on the label before picking fruit.

tomato_late_blight.cause: A fast-moving water mold (Phytophthora infestans, the pathogen behind the Irish potato famine) that spreads explosively in cool, wet weather - greasy grey-green blotches on leaves that turn brown and papery within days, sometimes with white fuzzy growth underneath.
tomato_late_blight.homeRemedy: This one moves too fast for home remedies to keep up with once established - remove and destroy (bag, don't compost) infected leaves and whole plants immediately if it's spreading, since spores travel on wind and rain to neighboring plants and gardens. Water only at the soil line, never overhead, and increase spacing/staking for airflow. Prevention matters far more than treatment here.
tomato_late_blight.marketRemedy: Copper fungicide (copper hydroxide or copper octanoate, e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide or Monterey Liqui-Cop) or chlorothalonil (e.g. Bonide Fung-onil) are the only products reliably available to home gardeners, and they only PREVENT new infection - they won't cure leaves already blighted. Start spraying every 5-7 days as soon as cool, wet weather sets in or late blight is reported in your area (check your local extension office's blight alerts), and remove infected material regardless of spraying.

tomato_bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria (Xanthomonas species) that enter through wounds and pores and spread via splashing water, wet tools, and handling wet plants - small, dark, greasy-looking spots with yellow halos on leaves and scabby spots on fruit.
tomato_bacterial_spot.homeRemedy: Remove affected leaves and any fallen debris, and disinfect pruning shears/tools with rubbing alcohol or a 10% bleach solution between plants. Water at the soil only and avoid working with plants while they're wet. Home remedies like baking soda are far less effective against bacteria than against fungi, so don't rely on them alone here.
tomato_bacterial_spot.marketRemedy: A copper-based bactericide (copper hydroxide, or copper hydroxide + mancozeb combo products) is the standard home-garden option - e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide or Southern Ag Liquid Copper Fungicide - applied every 7-10 days starting at first symptoms, since copper suppresses spread rather than curing existing spots. Biofungicides containing Bacillus subtilis (e.g. Serenade Garden) can be alternated with copper for better control with less resistance risk. Disinfect tools and avoid overhead irrigation going forward, since copper resistance builds quickly if it's the only tool used.

tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.cause: A fungus (Septoria lycopersici) that survives in soil and plant debris over winter, starting on the lowest/oldest leaves as small circular spots with dark borders and tan centers, often dotted with tiny black specks.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.homeRemedy: Prune off spotted lower leaves as soon as they appear and clear fallen leaf debris from the soil surface. Mulch to block soil splash, and water at the base only. A weekly spray of 1 tbsp baking soda + 2.5 tbsp vegetable oil + 1 tsp liquid soap per gallon of water helps suppress mild cases - spot-test a leaf first since baking soda can scorch in strong sun.
tomato_septoria_leaf_spot.marketRemedy: Chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicides (e.g. Bonide Fung-onil or Southern Ag Liquid Copper Fungicide) are the standard home-garden treatment, applied every 7-10 days from first symptoms through the season since septoria keeps producing new spores on infected leaves all summer. At season's end, remove and destroy all plant debris (don't till it into soil) since the fungus overwinters there and reinfects next year's crop.

tomato_leaf_mold.cause: A fungus (Passalora fulva) that thrives in high humidity (above ~85%) and poor air circulation, most common in greenhouses, tunnels, or crowded plantings - pale yellow patches on the top of leaves with fuzzy olive-green to grey mold underneath.
tomato_leaf_mold.homeRemedy: Space plants further apart and prune lower/interior growth to open up airflow, ventilate greenhouses/tunnels aggressively, and switch to soil-line watering (drip or soaker hose) instead of overhead sprinklers. Remove affected leaves promptly. A baking soda spray (1 tbsp baking soda + 2.5 tbsp vegetable oil + 1 tsp liquid soap per gallon) every few days can help manage mild cases.
tomato_leaf_mold.marketRemedy: A copper fungicide or chlorothalonil spray (e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide or Bonide Fung-onil) every 7-10 days helps once humidity can't be brought down on its own, particularly in greenhouse settings. Potassium bicarbonate fungicides (e.g. GreenCure, MilStop) are another effective, low-toxicity option for fungal leaf diseases like this one. If it recurs every season, look for leaf-mold-resistant tomato varieties (marked with 'Cf' resistance genes).

tomato_spider_mites.cause: Tiny sap-sucking pests (usually two-spotted spider mites) that thrive in hot, dry, dusty conditions - fine stippled/pale speckling on leaves, bronzing, and fine webbing on undersides and between leaves in heavier infestations.
tomato_spider_mites.homeRemedy: Blast the tops and undersides of leaves forcefully with a strong stream of water every 2-3 days to physically knock mites and eggs off - this alone controls light infestations. Follow with a homemade insecticidal soap (1 tbsp mild liquid soap such as castile or Ivory - not detergent - per quart of water), spraying thoroughly including leaf undersides in early morning or evening. Keep the plant consistently watered, since drought-stressed plants attract and support far more mites.
tomato_spider_mites.marketRemedy: Neem oil (e.g. Bonide Neem Oil, Garden Safe) or a ready-made insecticidal soap (e.g. Safer Brand Insecticidal Soap) applied every 5-7 days for 2-3 rounds breaks the egg-to-adult cycle - spray in the evening/cool part of the day since oils can scorch leaves in direct sun. For heavier infestations, a miticide containing spinosad (e.g. Monterey Garden Insect Spray) is effective and gentler on beneficial insects than broad-spectrum pesticides. Rotate between neem, soap, and spinosad rather than repeating one, since mites build resistance quickly.

tomato_target_spot.cause: A fungus (Corynespora cassiicola) that produces distinctive brown, concentric 'target' or bullseye-ringed spots, favored by warm, humid weather and wet foliage - easily confused with early blight and septoria, but the rings are usually larger and more defined.
tomato_target_spot.homeRemedy: Remove affected leaves promptly and avoid wetting foliage when watering - drip irrigation or watering at the base only makes a big difference. Improve airflow with wider spacing and by pruning lower branches. A weekly baking soda spray (1 tbsp baking soda + 2.5 tbsp vegetable oil + 1 tsp liquid soap per gallon of water) can help suppress mild, early cases.
tomato_target_spot.marketRemedy: Chlorothalonil or copper-based fungicides (e.g. Bonide Fung-onil or Southern Ag Liquid Copper Fungicide) applied every 7-10 days from first symptoms are the standard home-garden defense - the same spray program often used for early blight and septoria, since all three favor the same warm, humid, wet-leaf conditions. Clear and destroy plant debris at season's end since the fungus overwinters on it.

tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: A virus (Tobacco Mosaic Virus or Tomato Mosaic Virus) causing mottled light/dark green patterns, curling, and stunted growth. It spreads through handling (including residue from tobacco products) and via insects like aphids. There is no cure once a plant is infected.
tomato_mosaic_virus.homeRemedy: There's no home treatment that cures a virus - remove and destroy (don't compost) infected plants to protect the rest of the garden, since the virus persists in plant debris and even dried tobacco. Wash hands thoroughly with soap (not just water) and disinfect tools with a 10% bleach or rubbing-alcohol solution between plants, especially after touching infected foliage. Avoid smoking or handling tobacco products around plants, and control aphids going forward since they're a common vector.
tomato_mosaic_virus.marketRemedy: No spray, fungicide, or pesticide cures a viral infection - anything marketed as a plant 'virus cure' isn't genuine. The real market-side action is prevention for next season: buy certified virus-free/resistant seed or transplants (look for 'ToMV' resistance on the seed packet), and use an insecticidal soap or neem oil to keep aphid populations down since they spread the virus between plants. Yellow sticky traps also help monitor and reduce aphid numbers.

tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.cause: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV), spread exclusively by the silverleaf/sweetpotato whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) - causes yellowing, upward leaf curling, and severely stunted growth with little to no fruit. Like other plant viruses, there is no cure once infected.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.homeRemedy: Remove and destroy infected plants promptly to cut off the source of virus for whiteflies to keep spreading - they can't be cured or nursed back. Use yellow sticky traps near plants to catch and monitor adult whiteflies, and check the undersides of leaves regularly (eggs/nymphs cluster there) so you catch an outbreak before it spreads. Reflective mulch (aluminum foil or silver plastic mulch around the base) has been shown to repel whiteflies from landing on plants in the first place.
tomato_yellow_leaf_curl_virus.marketRemedy: Since there's no cure, market-side treatment targets the whitefly vector, not the virus itself: insecticidal soap or neem oil sprayed on leaf undersides every 5-7 days knocks back whitefly populations with low toxicity to beneficial insects. For heavier infestations, a systemic insecticide containing imidacloprid (soil-applied, labeled for tomato) protects new growth from whiteflies feeding on it. For future seasons, look for TYLCV-resistant tomato varieties (seed packets marked 'TYLCV resistant' or with 'Ty' resistance genes) - resistance is currently the single most effective tool against this disease.

apple_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
apple_healthy.homeRemedy: Keep the area under the canopy raked clear of fallen leaves and fruit through the growing season and especially in fall, since most apple diseases overwinter in that debris. Prune every winter (while dormant) to open up the center of the tree for airflow and sunlight, and water deeply but infrequently at the root zone rather than on the leaves.
apple_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. A dormant-season copper spray in late winter (before buds break) is a cheap, standard preventive step for home orchards, especially if scab or rust has shown up on this tree or nearby apple/crabapple/cedar trees before. A balanced fruit-tree fertilizer in early spring supports healthy new growth.

apple_scab.cause: A fungus (Venturia inaequalis) that overwinters in fallen leaves and infects new leaves and fruit in cool, wet spring weather - olive-green to dark brown velvety spots on leaves, and corky, scabby lesions on fruit.
apple_scab.homeRemedy: Rake up and destroy (bag or burn, don't compost) all fallen leaves in autumn - this is the single most effective non-chemical step, since the fungus overwinters and releases spores from that leaf litter the following spring. Prune to open the canopy for airflow and faster leaf-drying after rain or dew.
apple_scab.marketRemedy: Myclobutanil (e.g. Spectracide Immunox, Fertilome F-Stop) is the most effective home-garden fungicide for scab, alongside captan or wettable sulfur as organic-leaning options. Spray on a 7-10 day schedule starting at green tip (as buds first open) through several weeks of wet spring weather, since scab is a preventive-only target - once spots appear on a leaf, that leaf can't be un-infected, but spraying protects the rest of the tree's new growth.

apple_black_rot.cause: A fungus (Botryosphaeria obtusa) that infects through wounds, dead wood, and old cankers - purple-bordered brown leaf spots ('frog-eye leaf spot'), plus rotting fruit and sunken cankers on branches.
apple_black_rot.homeRemedy: Prune out dead, cankered, or diseased wood during dry weather (fungal spores spread easily in wet conditions) and destroy the prunings - cankers are the main source of new infection each year. Remove mummified fruit left on the tree or ground, since it also harbors the fungus over winter.
apple_black_rot.marketRemedy: Captan or myclobutanil-based fungicides, applied on the same schedule used for apple scab (they're often managed together with one combined spray program), help protect fruit and new growth. Because black rot mainly spreads from cankers and dead wood, sanitation (pruning + removing mummies) matters more here than spraying alone - a well-sprayed tree with cankers left in place will keep reinfecting itself.

apple_cedar_apple_rust.cause: A fungus (Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae) with a two-host life cycle that alternates between apple/crabapple trees and Eastern red cedar or juniper trees - bright orange-yellow spots on leaves, sometimes with small tube-like structures on the leaf underside.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.homeRemedy: If practical, remove Eastern red cedar or juniper trees within a few hundred feet, since the fungus can't complete its life cycle on apple alone and needs a nearby cedar/juniper host - though spores can travel over a mile, so this only helps with junipers on your own property. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn, and choose rust-resistant apple varieties for new plantings.
apple_cedar_apple_rust.marketRemedy: Myclobutanil (e.g. Spectracide Immunox) is the most effective home-garden fungicide for cedar apple rust - copper and sulfur give only partial control, and captan doesn't work well against rust at all, so myclobutanil is worth prioritizing here specifically. Apply starting at pink bud (just before bloom) and continue every 7-10 days through early summer while orange telial horns are visible on nearby junipers.

cherry_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
cherry_healthy.homeRemedy: Prune in summer rather than winter for cherries specifically (reduces the risk of certain canker diseases entering through pruning wounds), and keep the canopy open for airflow. Water deeply at the root zone and avoid wetting foliage, especially late in the day.
cherry_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. If powdery mildew has been an issue on this tree in past seasons, a preventive sulfur or potassium bicarbonate spray at the first sign of new, tender growth in spring can head it off before it starts.

cherry_powdery_mildew.cause: A fungus (Podosphaera clandestina) that thrives in warm days, cool nights, and shaded/crowded conditions - a white to grey powdery coating on leaves and shoot tips, especially new growth, without necessarily needing wet leaves to spread (unlike most other fungal diseases).
cherry_powdery_mildew.homeRemedy: Prune to open up the canopy and increase airflow and light penetration, and avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes exactly the soft, tender new growth this fungus prefers. A milk spray (1 part milk to 2-3 parts water, sprayed weekly on new growth) has real research support as a mild fungicide for powdery mildew, as does a baking soda spray (1 tbsp baking soda + 2.5 tbsp vegetable oil + 1 tsp liquid soap per gallon of water).
cherry_powdery_mildew.marketRemedy: Wettable sulfur (applied every 7-10 days) is the standard home-orchard treatment, or potassium bicarbonate products (e.g. Monterey Bi-Carb, GreenCure) as a gentler organic option that also kills existing mildew rather than only preventing new infection. Never apply sulfur within about 2-3 weeks of an oil spray (dormant or horticultural oil) - the combination can burn foliage.

peach_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
peach_healthy.homeRemedy: Prune annually in late winter/early spring to maintain an open center for airflow and sunlight, and clean up fallen leaves and fruit through the season. Water deeply at the root zone, especially during fruit development, and avoid wetting the leaves or trunk.
peach_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. A dormant copper spray at leaf-fall in autumn (not during the growing season, since copper can scar/russet peach fruit and foliage if applied later) is the standard preventive step for stone fruit orchards, especially if bacterial spot has appeared on this tree before.

peach_bacterial_spot.cause: Bacteria (Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni) that overwinter in bark cracks and bud scales and spread via wind-driven rain - small, dark, angular spots on leaves that often fall out leaving a 'shot-hole' look, plus sunken, pitted spots on fruit.
peach_bacterial_spot.homeRemedy: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizer, which encourages the soft, susceptible new growth bacteria prefer, and prune to improve airflow so leaves dry faster after rain. Rake up fallen, infected leaves - there's no effective home/organic spray once the tree is actively growing, so sanitation and correctly-timed copper (below) matter more here than for most other diseases.
peach_bacterial_spot.marketRemedy: Timing matters more than product choice here: a copper-based bactericide (e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide, Southern Ag Liquid Copper Fungicide) should be applied at leaf-fall in autumn and again in early spring before buds swell (the dormant season) - copper applied during the growing season, directly on leaves or fruit, commonly causes russeting/scarring on peach. There is no effective in-season rescue treatment for home growers; management is almost entirely about correctly-timed dormant sprays plus resistant varieties for new plantings.

grape_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
grape_healthy.homeRemedy: Keep the canopy pruned and trained (trellised) for airflow and sun exposure, and keep the ground under the vine clear of fallen leaves and mummified fruit through the season, since most grape diseases overwinter there. Water at the root zone, not overhead.
grape_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. If black rot or esca has appeared on this vine or nearby vines before, a preventive copper or mancozeb spray from bud break through about 4 weeks after bloom is the standard home-vineyard schedule.

grape_black_rot.cause: A fungus (Guignardia bidwellii) that overwinters in mummified fruit and infected canes - reddish-brown circular leaf spots, and fruit that shrivels into hard black 'mummies' still hanging on the vine.
grape_black_rot.homeRemedy: Remove and destroy mummified fruit, diseased tendrils, and prunings from both the vine and the ground - this is the single biggest lever, since next year's infections come almost entirely from mummies left behind. Keep the canopy open and weed-free for faster drying after rain.
grape_black_rot.marketRemedy: Captan, copper, or mancozeb fungicides (mancozeb is often the preferred home-garden protectant here) applied from bud break through about 4 weeks after bloom - the critical infection window - give the best control. Once berries mature past that window they're largely resistant, so early-season spraying matters far more than late-season.

grape_esca.cause: A complex of wood-rotting fungi that infect through pruning wounds and slowly colonize the trunk and cordons over years - tell-tale 'tiger-stripe' interveinal yellow/red streaking on leaves, and dark spotted, dried-looking berries. There is no cure once a vine's trunk is infected.
grape_esca.homeRemedy: There's no home treatment that reverses esca - it's a trunk disease, not a leaf-surface fungus a spray can reach. Prune during dry weather only (infection spreads through wet pruning wounds), and consider 'double pruning' or delaying final pruning cuts until later in dormancy when the vine is less susceptible. Severely declining vines are usually best removed and replaced rather than nursed along.
grape_esca.marketRemedy: No fungicide cures esca - sprays target leaf/fruit fungi, not the internal trunk rot. Wound-sealant/pruning-paste products applied immediately after pruning can reduce new infections entering through fresh cuts, which is the main preventable entry point. For a badly declining vine, trunk renewal (cutting back hard to healthy wood and retraining a new trunk) is the closest thing to a fix.

grape_leaf_blight.cause: A fungus (Pseudocercospora vitis / Isariopsis) causing angular brown spots on leaves that can merge and cause early defoliation in warm, humid weather.
grape_leaf_blight.homeRemedy: Remove and destroy fallen leaves and prunings at season's end, since the fungus overwinters there. Improve canopy airflow through pruning and training, and avoid overhead watering.
grape_leaf_blight.marketRemedy: The same copper or mancozeb spray program used for black rot (bud break through several weeks post-bloom) generally controls this too, since home vineyards typically manage all the common grape leaf fungi on one combined schedule rather than spraying for each separately.

olive_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
olive_healthy.homeRemedy: Prune to keep the canopy open for airflow and sunlight (olive fungal diseases thrive in shaded, humid canopies), and clear fallen leaves from around the base. Water deeply but infrequently - olives are drought-tolerant and overwatering encourages root and fungal problems.
olive_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. If peacock spot has been an issue on this tree before, a preventive copper spray in late autumn before winter rains (repeated in spring if wet weather continues) is the standard preventive step for home olive growers.

olive_peacock_spot.cause: A fungus (Venturia oleaginea / Spilocaea oleagina) causing distinctive dark, concentric-ringed 'peacock feather' spots on the upper leaf surface, favored by mild, wet winters and shaded, poorly-ventilated canopies.
olive_peacock_spot.homeRemedy: Prune to open up the canopy - this fungus thrives in shaded, still air more than almost any other factor. Rake and remove fallen leaves, since they carry the fungus into the next wet season.
olive_peacock_spot.marketRemedy: Fixed copper fungicide (e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide) is the standard and most reliable treatment - apply preventively in late October/autumn before winter rains begin, and again in spring if wet weather persists, for about 4 sprays a year spaced 10-14 days apart. Copper only protects healthy leaves going forward; it won't remove existing spots.

olive_bud_mite.cause: A microscopic mite (Aculus olearius) that feeds on buds, leaves, and developing fruit, causing distorted growth, silvery/bronzed leaf discoloration, and occasionally reduced fruit set.
olive_bud_mite.homeRemedy: This pest rarely causes serious tree damage or a meaningful harvest loss even at noticeable infestation levels, so for a home tree, monitoring rather than aggressive treatment is often enough. Pruning out heavily distorted growth and keeping the tree otherwise healthy (proper watering, not over-fertilizing with nitrogen) helps it outgrow mild infestations.
olive_bud_mite.marketRemedy: Wettable sulfur is the standard treatment if several consecutive years of noticeably reduced harvest make treatment worthwhile - applied in early spring as buds begin to swell. Since bud mites usually aren't damaging enough to justify spraying every year, treat based on actual harvest impact rather than on a fixed schedule.

banana_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
banana_healthy.homeRemedy: Remove old, dead, or dying leaves regularly (they're a major source of fungal spores for the diseases below) and keep plants spaced for airflow. Water at the base and avoid wetting leaves late in the day.
banana_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. If Sigatoka has been a recurring problem in your area, a preventive copper or neem oil spray during the wet season can help keep new leaves ahead of infection.

banana_sigatoka.cause: A fungus (Mycosphaerella/Pseudocercospora species) causing streaked, then spreading brown/black spots on leaves that merge and can kill large sections of leaf tissue in warm, humid, wet conditions - one of the most damaging banana diseases worldwide.
banana_sigatoka.homeRemedy: Remove and destroy heavily spotted or dead leaves regularly to reduce the spore source (this alone meaningfully slows spread in a home planting), and space/prune surrounding vegetation to improve airflow and sun penetration around the plant.
banana_sigatoka.marketRemedy: Contact fungicides (mancozeb or chlorothalonil) applied preventively during wet/humid periods, or a systemic fungicide (propiconazole or tebuconazole) for better curative action once spots appear, are the standard options. Neem oil (1-2 tbsp per liter of water) is a lower-toxicity option for light infections. Rotate between different fungicide classes if spraying repeatedly, since Sigatoka fungi are known to develop resistance quickly to any single product used alone.

banana_cordana.cause: A fungus (Cordana musae) causing oval, pale-centered spots with a yellow halo, usually less aggressive than Sigatoka but still capable of merging into larger blighted patches on stressed plants.
banana_cordana.homeRemedy: Remove affected leaves promptly and keep the planting well-spaced for airflow. This disease is usually a secondary/opportunistic problem on already-stressed plants, so consistent watering and nutrition go a long way toward prevention.
banana_cordana.marketRemedy: Copper oxychloride or mancozeb sprays in more severe cases are the standard treatment, applied to new growth every 2-3 weeks until symptoms subside. Milder cases often resolve once the underlying plant stress (usually drought or nutrient deficiency) is corrected.

banana_pestalotiopsis.cause: A fungus (Pestalotiopsis species) that typically enters through leaf-tip wounds or damage, causing grey-brown spots with a darker border, often starting at leaf edges/tips.
banana_pestalotiopsis.homeRemedy: Trim and destroy damaged or spotted leaf tissue (this fungus often follows physical wind/tear damage, so reducing wind exposure or providing a windbreak helps prevent entry points). Keep plants well-watered and fertilized, since this is largely an opportunistic fungus on stressed tissue.
banana_pestalotiopsis.marketRemedy: Copper-based fungicides applied to new growth control most cases; treatment is rarely needed beyond removing damaged leaf tissue unless the planting is under ongoing wind/mechanical stress that keeps creating new entry wounds.

citrus_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
citrus_healthy.homeRemedy: Water deeply at the root zone and avoid wetting foliage. Prune out dead/crossing branches for airflow, and check new flush growth regularly for the tiny whitefly-like Asian citrus psyllid, the insect that spreads citrus greening - catching it early matters far more for citrus than for most other trees, since greening has no cure once a tree is infected.
citrus_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. A balanced citrus-specific fertilizer in early spring and again in early summer supports strong flush growth. If canker or black spot has occurred on this tree before, a preventive copper spray at each new leaf flush is the standard home-grower schedule.

citrus_canker.cause: Bacteria (Xanthomonas citri) that enter through wind-driven rain, wounds, and leaf miner damage - raised, corky, scab-like lesions with a yellow halo on leaves, stems, and fruit.
citrus_canker.homeRemedy: Prune and destroy visibly infected shoots and leaves during dry weather (wet-weather pruning spreads the bacteria on tools and hands), and disinfect tools with a bleach or alcohol solution between cuts. A windbreak (hedge or fence) reduces wind-driven rain spread, one of the main ways canker moves between trees.
citrus_canker.marketRemedy: Copper-based bactericides (e.g. Bonide Copper Fungicide) applied at each new leaf flush, roughly every 3 weeks through the growing season, are the standard control - copper prevents new infections but won't cure existing lesions. There is no cure for a badly infected tree; in severe, spreading cases removal is sometimes the only option to protect nearby citrus.

citrus_black_spot.cause: A fungus (Phyllosticta citricarpa) that overwinters in fallen leaf litter and infects fruit and leaves during warm, wet weather - small, dark, freckle-like spots on fruit rind and leaves.
citrus_black_spot.homeRemedy: Rake up and destroy fallen leaves regularly, especially through fall and winter - like apple scab, this fungus survives specifically in leaf litter on the ground and reinfects the tree from there each spring. Prune for airflow to speed leaf-drying after rain.
citrus_black_spot.marketRemedy: Copper fungicide sprayed every 3-4 weeks from the first spring flush through harvest is the standard home-garden control, since this disease is preventive-only - it protects new growth and fruit but won't remove existing spots.

citrus_greening.cause: Huanglongbing (HLB), a bacterial disease (Candidatus Liberibacter) spread by the Asian citrus psyllid - causes blotchy yellow mottling, stunted and bitter/misshapen fruit, and progressive tree decline. There is currently no cure once a tree is infected.
citrus_greening.homeRemedy: There's no home treatment that cures HLB. The most effective home-garden action is removing and destroying an infected tree promptly, since it becomes a continual source of bacteria for psyllids to spread to every other citrus tree nearby. Inspect new growth regularly for the Asian citrus psyllid (a small, tilted-when-feeding insect) on any remaining or new citrus trees.
citrus_greening.marketRemedy: No product cures HLB - be skeptical of anything marketed as a citrus greening 'cure.' Market-side action targets the psyllid vector instead: insecticidal soap or neem oil on new flush growth, or a systemic soil-drench insecticide (imidacloprid, labeled for citrus) for heavier psyllid pressure. For replanting, buy only certified disease-free nursery stock - HLB also spreads through infected planting material.

fig_healthy.cause: No signs of disease detected in this photo.
fig_healthy.homeRemedy: Water deeply and consistently, especially during fruit development (irregular watering causes fruit-drop and splitting more often than disease does), and keep fallen leaves and fruit cleared from the base. Prune in winter dormancy to maintain airflow.
fig_healthy.marketRemedy: No treatment needed. Figs are generally low-disease trees when well-watered and not overcrowded - most issues that do appear are more often environmental (irregular watering, poor drainage) than pathogenic.

fig_infected.cause: This photo shows signs of infection, but figs are affected by several distinct diseases (fig rust, fig leaf spot/Cercospora, fig mosaic virus) that can look similar in early stages - this model flags 'infected' generally without distinguishing which one.
fig_infected.homeRemedy: Remove and destroy affected leaves, and clear fallen leaf litter from the base - most fig fungal diseases overwinter there regardless of which specific one it is. Improve airflow through pruning and avoid wetting foliage when watering.
fig_infected.marketRemedy: A general copper fungicide is a reasonable first step for most fungal fig leaf problems and is safe to try while you get a firmer diagnosis. Since the specific disease isn't identified here, take a clear photo (or the leaf itself) to a local nursery or agricultural extension office if it spreads or doesn't respond - fig mosaic virus in particular has no chemical treatment and needs a different response (remove the plant) than a fungal spot would.

unknown.cause: This photo doesn't clearly match a condition the model was trained to recognize - it might be a different plant, a non-tomato issue, healthy foliage under unusual lighting, or a physical/environmental problem (sunscald, nutrient deficiency, herbicide drift) rather than a disease.
unknown.homeRemedy: Try again with a clear, well-lit, close-up photo of a single affected leaf against a plain background, ideally showing both healthy and symptomatic tissue. If it keeps coming back unrecognized, look for patterns outside the model's known classes: purple-tinged leaves often mean phosphorus deficiency or cold stress, and yellowing between leaf veins (while the veins stay green) usually points to a nutrient deficiency rather than disease.
unknown.marketRemedy: No product should be applied blind. Take a photo (or the leaf itself) to a local nursery or your county/state agricultural extension office - most offer free or low-cost plant diagnostics and can identify problems a photo-based model can't, including soil-borne issues, nutrient deficiencies, and pests too small to show up clearly in a photo.
